The card returns all four ids in internal storage order, 3, 1, 4, 2, which is not sorted." width="100%"} Returns node IDs in the graph up to the specified limit. Node IDs are unique integers (`u64`) assigned to each node, useful for iterating over nodes or performing operations on specific nodes. The IDs come back in the graph's internal storage order, which is neither sorted nor the order in which nodes were added. Wrap the result in `sorted()` if you need ascending IDs, or use `get_node_creation_order()` for chronological order. Every node is included regardless of any current selection; use `get_selected_node_ids()` for the selected nodes only. Note that the default `limit=1000` silently truncates the result on larger graphs. When you need every node -- for example to loop over all nodes or build a mapping of IDs to labels -- pass `limit=None`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [limit]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1000]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of node IDs to return (default `1000`). The first `limit` IDs in storage order are returned, which are not necessarily the earliest-created or smallest IDs. Pass `None` to return all node IDs (warning: may be slow for large graphs). The default prevents performance issues when working with large graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs in internal storage order, containing at most `limit=` entries. Empty if the graph has no nodes. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} By default, `get_node_ids()` returns up to `1000` IDs -- plenty for typical graphs. Notice that the IDs are not in ascending order: ::: {#5e1cc0ff .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) ) ids = graph.get_node_ids() len(ids), ids ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (3, [2, 3, 1]) ``` ::: ::: Sorting the IDs and mapping them to labels gives a readable overview of the nodes: ::: {#bfcd6d2e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} {nid: graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in sorted(graph.get_node_ids())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {1: 'A', 2: 'B', 3: 'C'} ``` ::: ::: Passing `limit=` caps the result, which is useful for a quick preview on larger graphs. The ten IDs returned are simply the first ten in storage order, not IDs `1` to `10`: ::: {#d85571b0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_nodes([f"Node_{i}" for i in range(100)]) graph.get_node_ids(limit=10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [44, 88, 25, 69, 6, 50, 94, 31, 75, 12] ``` ::: ::: On a graph with more than `1000` nodes the default limit truncates the result, so pass `limit=None` whenever you need every node: ::: {#49916800 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} big = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=1500) len(big.get_node_ids()), len(big.get_node_ids(limit=None)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (1000, 1500) ``` ::: :::
